faq.q: Why is my photo several MB?
faq.a: Modern phone cameras capture 12 megapixels or more, and every pixel costs bytes. A form needs only a tiny fraction of them.

faq.q: Can I convert MB to KB without losing quality?
faq.a: You lose only detail the form would never show. On screen, at the size the portal uses, a 100 KB version looks the same as the 3 MB original.

paras: In the binary system that Windows and most exam portals use, a kilobyte is 1024 bytes and a megabyte is 1024 kilobytes. Phones and Macs often show sizes in decimal units instead, where 1 MB is 1000 KB and 1 KB is 1000 bytes. So the same photo can show as 2.0 MB in your gallery and as 1,953 KB on a computer.

That gap matters at the edge of a limit. This MB to KB converter counts 1 KB as 1024 bytes and also keeps the file under the decimal reading of your limit, so a 50 KB target stays under 50,000 bytes and passes either way.
list: 0.5 MB = 512 KB (500 KB in decimal units)

sections.h2: What a 2 MB photo size really holds
paras: A 12-megapixel phone camera takes pictures of about 4000×3000 pixels, saved as JPG or HEIC files of 2–5 MB. That is far more than any form shows: a banking photo is only 200×230 pixels. Turning a 2 MB photo into 50 KB makes the file about 40 times smaller, and most of that comes from reducing the pixels, not from lowering the quality.

sections.h2: 1 MB photo size and other MB limits
paras: Some portals state a limit such as "maximum 1 MB" or "below 2 MB". If your photo is already under it, upload it as it is. If not, type 1000 as the target for a 1 MB cap or 2000 for 2 MB: the file stays under 1,000,000 or 2,000,000 bytes, which passes both readings.
